I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over forty years. My father farmed it before me, and his father before him. I know this land. The North China Plain has one way of doing things that works: winter wheat, then summer maize on the same fields. That's the rotation. That's what the soil knows, what the market wants, what the seed station sells, what my neighbors do. I'm not going to try something different at 65.

My two sons are in Shijiazhuang now. It's mostly me and my wife. We have about 10 mu of cropland. I can manage 10 mu at my age, barely.

For wheat, I'll plant in October after the maize harvest. I'll get the improved variety from the village seed station — the one they've been recommending the last few years. I've used it before and it did fine. I'll rotary till after maize, then sow. Fertilizer: I put down the base fertilizer before sowing, then top-dress in spring at jointing. Maybe a bit more nitrogen than the pamphlets say — my father always said the land needs feeding. Three irrigations: one before sowing to get good germination, one in late winter or early spring, one around heading. Two pesticide sprays — herbicide in winter, then something for rust and aphids before harvest.

For maize, I plant right after wheat harvest in June. No time to waste — the season is short. Hybrid seed, everyone uses hybrid now, the yield is just better. I'll direct seed or rotary till lightly. Maize gets summer rain mostly, but I'll irrigate twice if it's dry — at tasseling especially, that's the critical time my father told me. Fertilizer split between sowing and topdress at knee-high.

I don't experiment. I don't have money to lose on a failed new crop. I do what works.
